opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think analogy is really at the core of almost everything we do cognitively. That's a view I picked up from Doug Hofstadter when I was his graduate student, and the more I've thought about it over the years, the more convinced I've become. We tend to think of analogy as something rarefied, the kind of thing you see on an SAT test or in a famous scientific discovery, like seeing the atom as a little solar system. But really it's happening constantly, at every level, mostly without our noticing.

Think about how we recognize categories at all. When you see a chair you've never seen before and you know it's a chair, you're making a kind of analogy. You're mapping this new thing onto your prior experience and seeing what's essentially the same despite all the surface differences. Or when a friend tells you about a frustrating day and you say, "Oh, the same thing happened to me," you're not saying the details were identical. You're saying the gist was the same, the abstract structure of the situation. That ability to perceive "sameness" at an abstract level is what lets us take what we've learned in one situation and use it in another.

Language is full of this too. George Lakoff and Mark Johnson made the point decades ago that so much of our everyday language is metaphorical. We talk about time as money: we spend it, waste it, save it. We talk about arguments as war: we defend positions, attack claims, win or lose. Ideas are things we "grasp." We're "ahead" or "behind" schedule. These aren't just decorative figures of speech; they reflect how we actually structure abstract concepts in terms of more concrete, physical, embodied experience. We understand the unfamiliar by mapping it onto the familiar.

That's part of why I think analogy is so important for AI. The thing humans do so effortlessly, taking a concept and flexibly applying it to new situations, recognizing that two very different-looking things share deep structure, is exactly where AI systems have historically struggled. They can be extremely good within the distribution they were trained on, but that kind of robust abstraction and transfer is much harder. So for me, understanding analogy isn't a side topic. It's really central to understanding what intelligence is, and to understanding what's still missing in our machines.

r001.rationale: It describes analogy as seeing an abstractly similar gist or structure across situations whose details differ.

r002.rationale: It says analogy happens constantly in everyday cognition, mostly without people noticing.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a skeptic’s question about putting analogy “in the driver’s seat” or identify it as an analogy.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think analogy is really at the core of how we think, and I don't mean that in a metaphorical way. I mean it quite literally. When most people hear the word "analogy," they think of those SAT-style problems, you know, "hand is to glove as foot is to what?" Or they think of the kind of thing a scientist does when they say the atom is like a tiny solar system. But those are really just the most visible, explicit examples of something that's happening constantly, mostly below the level of our awareness.

Doug Hofstadter, who I did my PhD with, has this phrase that analogy is "the fuel and fire of thinking," and I've come to believe that's right. Every time you recognize a situation as being an instance of something you've seen before, you're making an analogy. If I walk into a coffee shop I've never been in and I know roughly what to do, where to stand, how to order, that's because I'm mapping this new situation onto past experiences that are similar in some abstract sense but different in all the details. The concepts we use are really built up out of these mappings.

And language is just saturated with it. We talk about "spending" time, or an argument being "attacked" or "defended," or someone being "in" love, as if love were a container. Lakoff and Johnson documented this extensively. These aren't flourishes we add on top of literal thought. They reflect how we structure abstract concepts in terms of more concrete, embodied experiences. Even something like understanding what "the same" means in a new context requires analogy. If I say "I'll have the same thing" at a restaurant, the waiter has to figure out what counts as the same in that situation, and that's a surprisingly subtle act of abstraction.

What fascinates me, and what got me into this in the first place, is that this ability is so effortless for humans and so hard to capture in machines. We can take a situation with lots of particulars and extract the essence of it, the thing that matters, and then recognize that same essence somewhere that looks superficially completely different. That flexible, context-sensitive abstraction is, I'd argue, the heart of what we mean by understanding. And it's exactly the thing that's been hardest to get right in AI, which is why I think analogy is such a useful lens for asking what current systems are actually doing when they appear to reason.

r001.rationale: The response says people extract a situation’s essence and recognize that same essence in a superficially different situation.

r002.rationale: It describes analogy as happening constantly, mostly below awareness, and gives everyday recognition of how to order in a new coffee shop as an example.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a skeptic’s question about putting analogy “in the driver’s seat” or identify that question as an analogy.

astra-6.text:
I think analogy is much more central to our thinking than we usually recognize. We tend to think of analogies as explicit comparisons—you know, “the atom is like a solar system”—but we’re constantly understanding new situations in terms of things we’ve experienced before. And that involves recognizing some shared structure, even when the details are quite different.

If somebody says, “That meeting was a train wreck,” you understand what they mean without imagining an actual train. You’re bringing aspects of one situation into another: things getting out of control, consequences nobody intended. Our everyday language is full of that kind of thing.

But it goes beyond language. Even recognizing that a new situation is an instance of something familiar requires us to decide what matters and what we can ignore. Two birthday parties can look completely different, yet we understand them as the same kind of event. I see a very close connection between that ability and analogy.

So, for me, analogy isn’t just a special reasoning technique that we occasionally use. It’s part of how we form concepts and make sense of the world. The difficult question is how we manage to find the relevant similarities, because almost any two things are similar in some way. What makes a similarity meaningful depends on the situation and on what we’re trying to do.

r001.rationale: It says people recognize shared structure across situations whose details differ.

r002.rationale: It describes people as constantly understanding new situations through past experience and says analogy is more central than we recognize, conveying routine, often unrecognized analogical thought.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a skeptic’s question about putting analogy “in the driver’s seat” or identify that phrasing as an analogy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think analogy is central to how we think, even though we often don’t notice we’re using it. We tend to associate analogy with an explicit comparison—saying that one thing is like another—but it’s much more pervasive than that. Whenever we encounter a new situation, we try to understand it in terms of something we already know. We’re asking, often unconsciously, “What is this like? Which aspects of my past experience apply here?”

In language, for example, if you say someone gave you a warm welcome, you’re connecting physical warmth with a kind of social experience. Those connections are so familiar that they don’t feel like analogies anymore.

But the interesting thing is that we’re not just matching superficial features. Two situations can look very different and still have the same underlying relationships. Recognizing those relationships—and figuring out which differences matter—is a big part of what makes human thinking flexible. So I don’t see analogy as some special form of reasoning that we occasionally use. I see it as a fundamental part of how we make sense of the world.

r001.rationale: It says different situations can share the same underlying relationships and that recognizing them is central to flexible thinking.

r002.rationale: It describes analogy as pervasive in everyday thought and says we often use it unconsciously when interpreting new situations.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a skeptic’s question or describe putting analogy “in the driver’s seat” as an analogy.
